en: *Commentary on the Essential Decisions Concerning the Western Regions*, Scroll One.
The general purport of this work is divided into four parts: first, whether the author is authentic; second, whether the sequence of the exposition is correct;

third, the main tenets of the correct exposition; and fourth, the definitive determination of the doctrinal intent (*śāstrārtha*). Regarding the first, whether the author is authentic: some say it is not [authentic].
This is the correct interpretation by Cien [Yixing]. Its textual form and underlying principles contradict his own school’s tenets;

that is, while he allows for the rebirth of ordinary beings and cites old translations, he does not rely on the new translations, and so forth. This refers to the Vinaya Master Jixian of Renhe Temple.
Upon examining the text, five points of doubt arise: first, the judgment regarding the ease or difficulty of rebirth contradicts the commentary on the *Sūtra on Rebirth in the Upper Heavens*;
second, the statement that "original enlightenment is perfectly luminous" deviates from the meaning of "initial enlightenment" (*ādikṣānti*) and *bodhi*;

third, the claim that "all return to the One Vehicle" does not accord with the true intent of the Three Vehicles; fourth, the judgment concerning whether one may regress from Tuṣita differs from the author's own previous commentary.

Regarding the presence or absence of the "Fivefold Samādhi" (Gojō) as a welcoming reception, the *Hokke-kyōmon* (Scripture on the Lotus Sutra) states that it was produced upon the back [of the scroll]. For these reasons, such interpretations are considered not to be the correct exegesis.

Some say that the *Gojō-jōju-shō* (Treatise on the Fivefold Samādhi) was fabricated by Ci'en (Xuanzang). They claim that during the reign of Emperor Kōnin, an imperial edict was issued to seek commentaries on the five schools;
the followers of Kōfuku-ji Temple recorded Ci'en’s interpretation and included it in their petition. Furthermore, the Vinaya Master An’ō composed the *Rokushū-shō* (Treatise on the Six Schools).
The *Shu-mulu* (Catalogue of Commentaries) attributes [this work] to Ci’en. Both Huixin and Yongguan were likewise titled "Ci'en.

My ancestor Heigou attained realization through this text and designated it as the authoritative teaching for the two schools; thus, we know that the *Ci'en* commentary is the orthodox interpretation.

As for the discussion on the meaning of the ordinary person’s rebirth, it describes the bodies and lands of that realm. All [who... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)
There are three schools of thought. The first holds that it is the enjoyment body for others (*parasaṃbhoga-kāya*). The second maintains it is exclusively a transformation body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*).

The third asserts it encompasses both types. Why do those who harbor doubts cling to a one-sided interpretation? If one relies on the first explanation regarding its meaning, one remains stuck in the narrow classification of the path of self-power alone.
Indeed, that which is drawn forth by the power of vows spans all levels, from the highest to the lowest; the five vehicles enter together, as taught by Daochuo.
Shandao, Master Gan, and others have collectively determined this meaning to be unique;

it is the ultimate discourse on what is encompassed by the Original Vow, that which is not adjudicated by the *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only) school, and that which has not been subsumed within the categories of Nature (*svabhāva*) and Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). How much more so when the text states:
"In the transformed land, one sees the transformed Buddha"—how obscure [the opposing view] would be! Furthermore, as for the sutras and treatises cited therein, they are difficult to scrutinize.
This explains the fundamental tenets of the sūtras and other scriptures; how could there be any dispute between "new" and "old" traditions as if they were opposites?

This refers to the principle that both the proponent and the opponent must mutually accept a common basis. As for the Vinaya master’s examination of the text, it can be understood from the text itself.

Regarding the second point, concerning whether the sequence of what was taught is not [as expected], there are two interpretations. First, it means that this is merely a direct presentation and does not necessarily follow a sequential order.
Furthermore, it is said: "It is not that there is no sequence. This refers to the first thirteen [chapters], which provide an exegesis and analysis leading to the conclusion.
The first [of these] clarifies the methods and tracks for practice, and so forth. Third, regarding the primary exposition of the essential meaning:

it causes people to abandon the [difficult path of] the holy way and take refuge in the Pure Land, thereby forever severing the cycle of rebirth and swiftly attaining the stage of non-retrogression; this is its grand design.

Furthermore, regarding the definitive determination of the fourfold intent (*abhiprāya*): that which is expounded throughout this entire work exclusively encourages rebirth in the Pure Land and instructs one to focus single-mindedly on the recitation of the Buddha's name;

thus, it takes "reciting the Buddha's name" as its primary tenet (*mūla*) and "rebirth in the Pure Land" as its ultimate goal (*prayojana*). This is precisely what is meant by the title, *The Essential Decision on the Western Paradise*.
*The Essential Decisions for Resolving Doubts Regarding the Western Region*:

This work provides instructions on the destination to which one should go. "Essential" (*yào*) means the pivot; "decisions" (*jué*) means determination; "resolving" (*shì*) means explaining; and "doubts" (*yí*) refers to uncertainty.

"Adherence" means being obstructed and failing to penetrate. "Penetration" (tōng) means comprehension. "Regulation" (guī) means measurement. This refers generally to a single gateway in the Western tradition;
by taking up its essential pivot, one establishes what is heterodox and what is orthodox, thereby unraveling the net of doubts and comprehending all difficulties.

It is the standard by which students rely to attain awakening. Whether in ancient or modern times, it remains unchanging; for a thousand years, people have followed it. Thus, it is called the "Universal Regulation" (Tōngguī). Furthermore—
This is indeed the essential resolution regarding the Western [tradition] and the universal rule for dispelling doubts.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Ji of Ci'en Monastery.
Ci'en Monastery is located in the Jinchang Ward; its original name was Jingjing Monastery. Emperor Gaozong [established it] for his mother, Empress Wende...
Empress Dowager Changsun was the consort of Emperor Taizong. While she was pregnant with Gaozong, after several days had passed without labor, she finally gave birth.
She then summoned the Court Physician Li Dongxuan to examine her pulse. Li reported, "Because the sagely son has grasped his mother’s heart with his hand, he cannot be born.
When Taizong asked how this could be, Li replied, "If you wish to spare the lives of both son and mother—"
The mother survived, but the son died. The Emperor brooded for a long time. The Empress submitted a memorial, saying, "If the son is retained, the imperial enterprise will prosper forever.
Taisong followed this petition. On the twenty-first day of the sixth month, Dongxuan received the imperial decree to take the holy son.
He then proceeded to apply acupuncture through her abdomen; the needle pierced her heart and reached her hand. The Empress Dowager passed away, and the Crown Prince was born immediately thereafter.
He later became the sovereign. His hand remained numb, and he constantly suffered from a throbbing pain in his palm. When the Emperor questioned his consorts, they did not respond.
Only when he inquired of the high ministers on a grand day of audience did they finally report this matter. Upon hearing it, the Emperor fainted and fell to the ground; after a long while, he...

Su said, "I, your humble servant, am unfilial that my compassionate mother passed away so early. To repay her profound kindness, I have issued an edict to construct Da Cien Temple and ordain one hundred monks;
I have built one Daoist observatory named Houtian Guan and one palace named Wangji Gong, where fifty Daoists are ordained.
This was in the tenth year of the Zhenguan era of Gaozong’s reign. The śramaṇa... [text ends]
It is said: "Diligent in Cessation. This means diligently cultivating the good and ceasing the evil; it is a general name for those who have left the household life.

The Master’s posthumous name was Kuījī, his courtesy name was Hóngdào, and his clan name was Wèichí. He was a native of Cháng'ān in Jīngzhào. He was the son of Wángzōng, a General of the Left Golden Myōng Guard under the Táng dynasty.
His mother was of the Pèi clan. She dreamed that she swallowed the lunar disc with her palm; upon waking, she became pregnant. When the months were full...
From birth, he was unlike other children. By the age of seventeen, he had entered the monastic community (*śramaṇa-vana*) and was appointed as a disciple of Master Xuanzang by imperial decree.

He initially resided at Guangfu Temple; subsequently, by a separate imperial edict, he was selected among those of exceptional intelligence and talent to enter Da Cien Temple, where he served Master Xuanzang in person, studied the languages of the five regions of India, resolved complex difficulties, and mastered the systematic principles [of Buddhist doctrine].
Thus it was; all who heard or saw him were moved to sighs of admiration and submission. Master Xuanzang said, "As for the Dharma of the Five Natures school, only you shall propagate it;
others shall not. He personally received the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, fully grasping their subtleties and expanding upon their source and flow.
In the first year of the Yongchun era (the Renwu year), he manifested illness, and on the thirteenth day of the eleventh month, he passed away.
In the Ci'en Translation Institute, he passed away at the age of fifty-one; his years of ordination (dharma-lakṣa) were not recorded.
He was buried north of Fancun in the North Canal, interred in the cemetery of the Tripiṭaka Master. "Zhuàn" means to compose, to narrate, or to create.

Looking up, I reflect that since Śākyamuni initiated his mission, he has extensively benefited all who possess the karmic affinity. His teachings have been propagated according to various regions, and all have equally received the nourishment of the Dharma.

Having personally encountered his sacred transformation, I have attained realization of the Three Vehicles through the Way. Yet, my merit being meager and my causal conditions sparse, I am exhorted to take refuge in the Pure Land.
The "Devadatta Chapter" states: "I expound the Mahāyāna teaching to deliver and liberate sentient beings from suffering.
The "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs Chapter" states: "The Dharma taught by the Buddha is like a great cloud; with rain of a single flavor, it moistens the flowers of humanity.

...The Buddha appears in the world and receives the regnal seal of the Dharma King; his transformation reaches the three thousandfold world system, universally delivering the multitudes, and he opens [the path] according to their capacities.

The guidance is such that no one remains without its benefit. Yet, while living in this world, those who possess superior conditions have already fulfilled their requirements; they personally receive the Sage’s transformation and each attains their own path.
However, in times of decadence, conditions are lacking and the veils of delusion become increasingly heavy. Those who are impoverished and devoid of merit have no means to practice personally.
How could one possibly endure this defiled land? This is the exhortation through practice; indeed, there is a profound reason for it.
Those who perform these practices should single-mindedly recite the name of Amitābha and dedicate all roots of goodness toward rebirth in that land, in accordance with the Original Vow of Amitābha.

"I vow to deliver all beings in the Sahā world: from those who manifest their final birth for a single lifetime above, down to those who recite the Name ten times at the moment of death below—should they be able to resolve with certainty, all shall attain rebirth in the Pure Land.

This entire section describes the intent of the *Amitābha Sūtra* (Kuan-ching) and the *Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*. Regarding the text of the Original Vow, it speaks generally of "ten" [recitations].

As for the term "Saha" used here, it is merely a reference to what is proximate. This is precisely what Daochuo of Tiantai meant when he explained that there are specific causes and conditions for this designation.

Scholars of the present day harbor particular doubts because the texts of various sutras and śāstras contain apparent contradictions; if these are not harmonized, the source of their uncertainty will never be severed.
I shall briefly set forth fourteen ways of explaining these turbulent currents, so that those of broad learning and penetrating talent may seek them out and attain awakening.
*Tuan*: This describes the swirling and eddying of waves and currents. It means that doubt and stagnation prevent one from proceeding, like water swirling and eddying.

To have extensive learning and a powerful memory is called "vast knowledge" (*boshi*). To have broad vision of the past and present, sufficient for taking effective action, is called a "capable talent" (*tongcai*).
The first, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, states: "If one sees me by means of form, or seeks me by means of sound, such a person follows a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata."
An objection is raised: The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras* state that seeking the Buddha through form and sound is judged to be a heterodox path.

Yet, the *Amitābha Sūtra* and others teach the visualization of the Buddha’s physical marks and the recitation of his name. Since seeking the Buddha does not depart from form and sound, how is it that these practices do not fall into the heterodox path?

The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the remaining two sūtras. To cause the sound not to cease and to cause the mind to contemplate the signs—that which is practiced by both mind and speech—means to focus exclusively on form and sound; therefore, it is called "not departing."

If one returns to the correct path, the Pure Land is something upon which one can rely; yet the sutras judge [certain practices] as heterodox. Even if one performs them, there is a fear of returning to the realm of Māra.

If the cause is the practice of a deviant path, the result will inevitably be the induction of a demonic realm. If practitioners do not understand this and take refuge [in such paths], they will transmigrate without end—how truly terrifying this is!
The two paths could not be decided; we pray that you distinguish between black and white.
"Black" refers to being dyed black.

[The interlocutor] replied: "The Master’s exposition of the teachings has many gates of meaning; each accords with the specific time and capacity [of the audience], and they are all equal without distinction."
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Because he is able to guide and transform immeasurable sentient beings, causing their suffering to be extinguished, he is titled the Great Master (*Mahāśāstṛ*).
Though a thousand paths proclaim diverse views, they all converge upon the same destination; therefore, it is said that there is no difference."
The Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras constitute one gate, while the Amitābha and other sūtras constitute another principle. "Gate" refers to that by which one enters;
"principle" refers to the destination toward which one proceeds. These aspects are manifested interchangeably in the texts.
Why is this? All Buddhas possess the three bodies. The Dharma-body is formless and lacks physical substance; it is neither color nor sound.
To apprehend it through the characteristics of color or sound is itself erroneous.
According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the pure dharma-realm is quiescent in all its characteristics and transcends the path of conceptual thought and verbal discourse;
therefore, it is said to be "formless and non-sonorous."
This is because those of the two vehicles and lesser bodhisattvas, upon hearing that the three bodies are not different, immediately assume they are identical in possessing form and sound.

Seeing only the physical characteristics of the *nirmāṇakāya*, they consequently hold that the *dharmakāya* is likewise so. Thus, they seek to perceive the *dharmakāya* through the marks of the *nirmāṇakāya*.
Since the subtle and profound principle of the ultimate truth is forever devoid of marks and sound, seeking to behold it through form and sound is therefore said to be erroneous.

As in the Sarvāstivāda school, they grasp the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the Buddha as the true Buddha; even those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) are thus deluded, hence it says "consequently grasping.
Because it is free from characteristics, quiescent, and transcends all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), it says "the subtle and refined is forever cut off. Someone may raise a doubt, saying:

"That the three bodies (*trikāya*) are not different does not seem to accord with what is discussed in the Dharma-characteristics school (*lakṣaṇayāna*). Now, the commentary reconciles this, saying: "This is not what is being said."
Regarding these marks (*lakṣaṇa*), they are simply the subsuming of marks back into their fundamental nature (*dharmatā*). Therefore, the *Fahua xuanzan* states:
"The response-body and transformation-body are not the true Buddha, nor are they the speakers of the Dharma; when one traces the merit back to its source, it is the Dharmakāya."

In the *Amitābha Sūtra* and other texts, those who are exhorted to practice mindfulness of the Buddha’s name, contemplate his marks, and seek rebirth in the Pure Land do so because, as ordinary beings with heavy obstructions, the Dharma-body is profound and subtle, and its essential nature is difficult to take as an object of focus.
Therefore, they are first taught to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, contemplate his form, and offer prostrations and praises. Through this, obstructions are severed and merit is generated;
as aspiration and practice support one another, they seek rebirth in the Pure Land, intending to encounter the transformation Buddhas there to serve as excellent conditions for non-retrogression.
According to the *Amitābha Sūtra* (Guān jīng), it is said that even possessing a complete physical form is already a difficult condition;

thus it states, "This is beyond the reach of the mental power of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), let alone the most wondrous True Body (*dharmakāya*). Regarding the contemplation of the Buddha’s physical body, this is as described in the *Amitābha Sūtra*.
The "Praise through Prostration" (*Lǐbài zàn*) is that which is exhorted in the *Treatise on the Exposition of the Dharma* (*Lùn wén*). Thus, there is the phrase "and so forth.

Regarding the Western Land, when discussing its retributive and transformational aspects, the various masters offer divergent interpretations; even the judgments of the present master are not uniform. As stated in the "Chapter on Buddha-lands": [text follows].
The West encompasses both the land of retribution and the land of transformation. In the *Shuji* (Commentary), it is identified as the "land of other-enjoyment.
Here, the judgment is made that these refer respectively to the land of transformation and the land of transformation for others; each merely describes one specific aspect.
For this reason, the enlightened persons of past ages all relied upon these teachings to contemplate the Buddha’s form and recite his name, seeking to behold his transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Hoping that at the moment of their death, he would personally come to welcome and guide them, they eventually moved Maitreya—the Lord of Transformation—to descend and meet them with his thought; thus, when their retribution ended, they ascended upon lotus flowers.
One will be reborn in that land immediately.
Those who have extensive insight into the past and present are called "men of penetration. Furthermore, the *Anleji* (Collection on Peace and Bliss) lists six great virtuous masters, stating:
"They are all divine mirrors of the two truths; they are the very pillars of the Buddha-dharma, and all together they have thoroughly examined the Mahāyāna," thus praising them.

They return to the Pure Land. For instance, when Dharma Master Tanluan was approaching the end of his life, both monastics and laypeople to the left and right of the monastery all saw banners and flowers illuminating the courtyard, and everyone smelled a wondrous fragrance as music welcomed him; he subsequently attained rebirth there.
Other great virtuous ones likewise had such manifest signs at the time of their deaths. Surely they were men of profound realization.
The initial mind and the subsequent object accord with principle without contradiction; reciting the name, contemplating the form, and so forth are none of them heterodox paths.
How can one harbor a single dogmatic attachment and fail to awaken to the Sage’s intent? Thus, diverse and confused doctrines proliferate, leading others into delusion.

Since both mindfulness and contemplation are incorrect, it is said that they are neither [correct]. "Fen-yun" (紛紜) describes a state of confusion and disorder. This not only harms oneself but also leads others into error.
How grave is the fault of such chaotic thoughts!

If you seek this essential decision, right and wrong will be clearly distinguished. Once hesitation has vanished, turn your heart toward these sublime practices; do not give rise to distracted thoughts, lest you fall back into the three miserable realms.
When oppressed by manifold sufferings, what use is it to regret? It would be too late.
According to the *Sūtra of Contemplation*, it says: "When all evils converge upon one, there will naturally be pressing urgency. At such a time, what can repentance avail?
Second, the *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra* states: "If there is a bhikṣu who perceives that the Buddha, Dharma, Saṅgha, or precepts are things to be grasped..."
They are the retinue of Māra and not my disciples; I am not their teacher, nor do I accept them.
This is the intent expressed throughout the ten chapters of this sutra, from which it never deviates.

An objection is raised: The *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra* states that to perceive a Buddha outside of one’s own mind is to speak of Māra; such a person is not the Buddha’s disciple, and the Buddha is not their teacher.

If this is so, then those who, according to the teachings of the Pure Land, exclusively practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name, contemplate the Buddha’s marks and signs, and seek rebirth in the Buddha-land, would not be disciples of the Buddha, nor would the Buddha be their teacher. How, then, could they receive the Buddha’s protective mindfulness and attain rebirth in the Pure Land?
In the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, it is said: "It is protected and remembered by all Buddhas. In the *Praise of the Sūtra*, it says:
"Through the empowerment of compassion, their minds are kept from distraction. Such are its defensive shields.
Looking up to investigate the two teachings, there is nothing that is not the Buddha’s word. Since the two explanations differ, how should one discern and judge between them? It is replied:

Although the traces of the teachings differ in ten thousand ways, they all return to the same single reality. Established according to the differences in the faculties [of sentient beings], their meanings diverge while their verbal expressions serve as the means of communication.

They accord with the power of expedient means and return to the reality of the One Vehicle; hence it is said they "converge in the same destination. They explain meanings according to what is appropriate, resulting in differences in verbal teaching;
hence it is said their "meanings are distinct. The Vinaya Master examined this passage and remarked: "This deviates from the meaning of the One Vehicle’s skillful means."
The *Jinhui* states: "Based on those of indeterminate nature, the convergence of the three [vehicles] into one is called 'converging equally toward the one reality.

Therefore, it does not depart from the true purport of the three vehicles. The *Fahua xuanzan* explains that this discourse concerns the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), and thus its meaning is consistently pervasive.

If one speaks of the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*), it refers to the fruit encompassing the cause; if one calls it the Bodhisattva-vehicle (*bodhisattvayāna*), it refers to the cause encompassing the fruit.
This is what is meant by that. This is precisely what is taught in the *Saṃgrahaṇī*; it is extensively discussed in that school.
As detailed in the *Praise* (the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*), if one carefully examines the two sutras, their wording differs while their principle is one.

What are they? Regarding the Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, and Precepts, there are three kinds of distinctions: first, the ultimate truth (paramārtha); second, the specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa); and third, the provisional maintenance (prajñapti).
In this separate explanation, the last of the five hindrances is omitted and will be fully recorded below.
When the essence of True Suchness (tathatā) is pure, the two hindrances perish; when fundamental awakening (mūla-avabodha) is perfectly luminous, it is itself the true Buddha.
According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is not subject to the increase of outflows (*āsrava*). Its nature is intrinsically pure and perfectly luminous;

although it possesses adventitious defilements (*āgantukakleśa*), its fundamental nature remains pure. Therefore, it is said: "The true essence is free from obstructions. This nature fundamentally possesses two bodies (*kāya*);

it is awakened and equal, inherently endowed with immeasurable virtues, and transcends all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Therefore, it is said: "Fundamental awakening is perfectly luminous. Or...
"It may be that the dharmas are inherently uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), and their original seeds are termed 'original enlightenment' (*mūla-awakening*).
This is based on the current master’s own interpretation of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, which preserves two meanings. The Vinaya Master examined this passage and stated:
"Does this not contradict the established meaning of 'initial awakening' (*ādi-bodhi*)? How could it be so?"
Maintaining its nature without change, the path of supreme wisdom is established. When Great Beings share this same condition, the myriad practices manifest; this is precisely the True Dharma.

Because it sustains all things with unchanging stability, it is said to be "unchanging. Because it serves as a model for sentient beings to develop understanding, it is called a "path" (*niyāma*). This is the path of all Buddhas.
By means of this, one attains Buddhahood; the Bodhisattva mounts it and reaches the stage of the Tathāgata. Therefore, it is called "the condition for accomplishment" (*chengyuan*).
Adorned by the dharmas of great merit, it has the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its support. Therefore, it is called "the attachment of practice" (*xingzhuo*).
It is in profound accord with principle and free from contention; this is the true monk.

Because he is neither identical to nor different from all phenomena, it is called "profound accord" (*mingfu*). Because he is the equal self-nature of all phenomena, it is called "conforming to principle" (*lihui*).
Because the paths of speech and thought are cut off and he is free from frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*), it is said that "contention is extinguished."
This is precisely the characteristic of true harmony and integration.
Its nature is pure, serene, and majestic; its substance is clean and free from defilement—this constitutes true precept-keeping.

As all outflows (*āsrava*) are forever exhausted and its nature is pure, perfect, and luminous, it is called "pure and majestic. Although there may be adventitious dust (*āgantuka-rajas*), its fundamental nature remains as such.
Because it is pure, it is called "stainless. This is the true essence of the pearl of precepts.
Based on this supreme meaning, it is called the "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-satya*).
Since this is not conventional, it is termed "supreme meaning."

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "If one can contemplate that the Three Jewels are eternally abiding and identical to the ultimate truth, this is precisely the supreme vow of all Buddhas. This is the meaning [of the passage].
This is the verse from the "Chapter on the Questions of the Great Assembly.

Regarding the distinct characteristics: the Buddha has three bodies, namely the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body. The Dharma has four aspects, namely Principle, Teaching, Practice, and Fruit.
The Sangha has two types, namely the conditioned and the unconditioned. As for the Precepts, they pertain to both the laity and the ordained.
The practitioner of the path of cultivation possesses the two types of upholding—cessation and action—which comprise all categories of precepts.
"Dharma" refers to the pure *tathatā* (suchness). "Retribution" refers to the two classes of enjoyment: that for oneself and that for others. "Transformation" refers to...

The "ten *zhang*" and the "sixteen *zhang*" refer to the manifestation of transformations according to the capacities of beings (*yathābhavyatā-vinirmita*). "Body" (*kāya*) is so named because it signifies the meaning of a collection of physical constituents.

"Teaching" (*dharma*) refers to the images that serve as the fundamental substance. "Principle" (*tattva*) refers to the true reality of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*). "Practice" (*caryā*) refers to the myriad practices of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). "Fruit" (*phala*) refers to *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*.
Because they provide a standard for conduct and sustain the arising of understanding, they are all termed "Dharma. The term "existence" (*bhava*) is used for the Śrāvakas.
The Tathāgata designated it as "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*), as seen in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. As for "practice," because it transcends the world, it is called the "cultivation of the path.
Guarding against wrongdoing through the three karmas and cultivating goodness through the ten branches are termed "cessation" and "action. Cessation refers to the precept of restraint;
action consists of the precepts of gathering virtue and benefiting sentient beings. The former, cessation, is upholding; action is transgression. The latter two refer to action.

To maintain [the precepts] is itself the cessation of transgression; therefore it is said that there are two types of maintenance: the maintenance of cessation and the maintenance of action. Because these encompass all categories, they are called "all.

Regarding the conclusion in the commentary on the "True Meaning" (Tattvārtha), it says "therefore it is said. This heading states "distinct characteristics"; the presence or absence of the heading and the conclusion are merely variations in the phrasing.

Those who practice merely the distinct characteristics in order to realize the ultimate truth, and who take their knowledge of these distinct characteristics alone to be the final goal, fail to awaken to the true source.
For those who study the precepts, these practices are all aids to the Path; the names and forms of the Buddha are manifestations that are not themselves the reality.

It was used to accommodate a few ordinary people as a temporary resting place; those of inferior intelligence did not understand this and mistakenly took it to be real. Therefore, the Buddha rebuked them, calling them followers of Māra.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that the explanation of the distinct characteristics of the Three Jewels is not ultimate, as it was taught for the sake of delivering śrāvakas and ordinary people.
Within the Buddha-nature itself, there already exist the Dharma and the Saṅgha; yet the ignorant and foolish fail to understand this, clinging instead to the appearance of difference.
Thus it is said, "They only know [the words] but do not awaken," and so forth. The precepts are like the great earth; all wholesome dharmas arise from them. To initiate...
Wisdom realizes the principle, while truth serves as its supporting condition. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "If one does not uphold the precepts, how can one ever perceive the Buddha-nature?

Those who wish to seek birth in the Pure Land should not say that it is "mixed. This is because as long as the fetters (*saṃyojana*) have not been severed, mixed birth may still occur;
however, once they have been extinguished, such mixing cannot arise. Thus, while [the fetters] have not yet been severed, they may occasionally manifest.

The mind of mindfulness of the Buddha is by nature contrary to the fetters; when the mind is correctly focused on the Buddha, the various fetters do not function. When there is an interval of interruption, if one does not guard against them, [they will arise].
This refers to arising; it does not speak of cessation. It means that there is no admixture.
Since the sages have exhausted all delusions, they find sufficient peace within this realm; they do not need to labor over mindfulness of the Buddha or seek rebirth in that land.
Those who doubt are deluded; this is not the thought of ordinary fools, but is the practice of the sages. Therefore, the formulation is as follows.

The *Pañcamasamyaksamādhisūtra* states: "If someone were to construct various temples and stupas, numbering in the infinite, it would not equal [the merit of] settling the mind in tranquil meditation for even a brief moment."
Furthermore, as the various Mahāyāna sūtras teach the principle of non-arising (*anutpāda*), they urge people to cultivate the path and train in wisdom.
A doubt arises: according to these teachings, the Buddha praises non-arising as being particularly supreme among all karmic practices;
yet, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* and others exhort one to go to the West, expressing weariness with this Sahā world and aspiring to be born in the Pure Land.
Birth is the master of affliction; when birth is exhausted, affliction is eliminated. To abandon birth while seeking birth causes the causes of affliction to gradually expand.

Why not practice the path of non-arising to awaken to the Dharma-body? To contemplate the Buddha’s physical form is due to a failure to understand the cause of birth; even if one were born in that land, how would it differ from this world?
Simply contemplate non-arising, and you will not be far from the Buddha. The mind is itself the Buddha—why rely on seeking elsewhere?
According to the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, that which is seen to arise and perish is entirely illusory and not truly existent. Birth is followed by aging;
because of aging there is death, along with grief, lamentation, suffering, and affliction. By merely severing birth, death naturally ceases.
If one does not know how to sever birth, one will ultimately never be free from death. This is the intended meaning here.
Since this practice is so focused, I hope you will kindly reveal its profound significance.
"Focused" means being self-reliant. To say that one acts for the sake of goodness oneself must surely contain a deep purport; I wish to hear it.

Tong said: "Practice arises from conditions and the teaching is established for the sake of benefiting sentient beings. That the explanations of the teachings differ is truly due to the diversity of capacities.
Why is this? Generally speaking, there are two broad types of root-capacities: first, those with deep karma; second, those with shallow practice. As for companions with deep karma..."
One may study non-arising; however, those of shallow practice must seek rebirth in the Pure Land.
Now, regarding the performance of karma, there are generally two paths: first, returning to the inverted state; second, transcendence and liberation.

Regarding those who speak with inverted understanding: although they study the Buddha-dharma, they do so merely for the sake of fame and reputation. They do not fear the perilous precipices of future birth and death;

they greedily seek superior understanding, yet instead become more firmly attached to the notions of self and person. They assert their own views as right while disparaging others, failing to restrain the three karmas, even as their speech proclaims the signless (*animitta*).

Attached to signs with fervent intensity, even if one studies the non-arising of phenomena, it becomes a mere craft. Upon seeing others recite the Buddha’s name, one immediately harbors perverse anger and resentment, causing practitioners to harbor thoughts of retreat and despondency.
Though one proclaims the wondrous medicine with the mouth, fearing they cannot take it, they instead consume various other volatile and poisonous drugs.
This mind constitutes karma; the mind then wanders aimlessly. Since the mind is not settled, one is unable to guard it.

They claim for themselves that they have attained understanding, yet upon investigation, they are found to be entirely devoid of it. Unaware, their lives come to an end, and they sink back into the cycle of birth and death.
They linger there, suffering, with liberation still far off. This is what is meant by "returning in reverse."
The "wondrous medicine" refers to the ambrosia of the eternally abiding true mark (*dharmatā*). Although one speaks of it with the mouth all day long, the mind has never tasted it;
hence it is said that one does not "take it. Not only does one fail to taste it, but one also clings to distinctions, thereby shortening the life of wisdom as if having consumed poison.
"To retreat" means to turn back. This karma appears to advance but actually regresses; hence it is called "returning in reverse."
Regarding what is called "transcendence," there are further two gates: first, non-arising; second, having signs.
As for non-arising, it means maintaining tranquility, discerning external conditions, and clearly knowing how to adopt and abandon based on the two characteristics of existence and non-existence.

Control the mind so that it proceeds spontaneously, dwelling in neither extreme. Whether speech or mental activity, examine them according to each circumstance. Whether encountering adversity or favorability, may the mind attain equanimity.
For instance, when swallowing burning coals or eating food, one experiences satisfaction and offers no complaint; eating fire or consuming charcoal is no different from swallowing food.
May all adverse and favorable conditions be treated in this same way, so that you are capable of enduring the Sahā world and dwelling therein for a long time.
They do not regress. This defiled land is transformed into a pure realm; since such power and efficacy exist, it constitutes liberation.

"Tian" (恬) means tranquility. "Can" (飡) refers to fine drink. Their mouths never utter a sigh of dissatisfaction. Even when swallowing fire or swallowing blades, their bellies are neither burned nor pierced.
If one matter is thus, the rest may be known accordingly; hence it is said that they are "all as such. These are all the deeds performed by those in superior stations.
If it is so, then principle abides in the Pure Land, even if it originates from a defiled land. True transformation turns rubble [into gold];
that the land is pure according to the mind is precisely what this refers to.
Regarding what is called "having signs" (*sanimitta*): because defilements, conditions, and hindrances are heavy, the signless (*animitta*) is difficult to accomplish.

If one remains in this world, all manner of sufferings accumulate; though one guards the mind within for stillness, it is dragged outward by external objects. As the mind pursues objects and shifts with them, the non-arising (*anutpāda*) is difficult to realize. Therefore, let the mind take refuge in a single Buddha.
Contemplate Amitābha; do not commit evil deeds. Seek rebirth in the Pure Land; when seeing others perform different practices, praise their virtues and bring them forth.

When hearing others speak of faults, do not give rise to contempt or disparagement. Bind the mind to a single point and direct one's thoughts afar toward the West. Let the three karmas support one another.
One will be born in that land through meditative concentration, and this also constitutes renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*).

Because the land is distinguished from all other directions, it is said to be "bound to one. Because the realm is established at a distance of one hundred thousand [yojanas], it is called the "conception of remoteness.
It is not merely that it is signless (*animitta*); because it is capable of leading to renunciation, it is said that "this also constitutes" it.

Fortunately, each person may verify the teachings through their own faculties; those who accord with them should practice accordingly. If one’s own karmic work is profound and one’s rank is non-retrogressive, there is no need to labor over grasping at signs, for one will surely be reborn in the Western Land.

As for those whose practice is shallow, they cannot yet avoid drifting in the cycle of birth and death; it is only when the essential realization of non-arising (*anutpāda*) is attained that one first escapes the entanglements of existence.
Though many recite "non-arising" with their mouths, among those who claim such realization, not even one in a hundred is found. If you wish to attain it...
Non-arising must necessarily depend upon the supreme object; therefore, one seeks the vision of the Buddha of Non-arising to serve as the condition for realization.

Having long dwelt in Jambudvīpa and constantly encountered virtuous friends, although one hears the True Dharma, the speaker is an ordinary person. Thus, though hearing it day and night, one has not yet realized the principle.

To recite "non-arising" with the mouth while one's actions are impure is called "not one. Alternatively, when the mind and mouth differ and words and deeds contradict each other, it may also be termed "not one."
The *Taima Sūtra* states: "To preach the Dharma all day long without being able to lead others to realize cessation (*nirodha*) or cultivate the Path is mere frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*);
it is not the seeking of the Dharma. Even if one were to encounter virtuous friends in a future life and give rise to causes based on the present, it would still result in frivolous proliferation.

It is better to seek rebirth in the Pure Land to first sever the cycle of saṃsāra and enter the Jewel Forest, where upon hearing the true words of the sublime Dharma, one attains the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)."
One should contemplate its perfect luminosity;

day and night, one speaks and listens, yet realization remains undivided. Cause and effect resonate like echoes, yet they turn into mere conceptual proliferation. Exhausting oneself from night until day, one labors in vain.
Therefore, it is said that this is "not as good as" [the former]. Because one is about to transcend the three realms, it is said to be "temporarily severed."
This ultimately fulfills the fruit; hence it is called "perfectly luminous" (*yuanming*). The *Contemplation Sūtra* states: "The Jewel Forest of Radiance expounds the wondrous Dharma.
Upon hearing it, one immediately awakens to the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and even attains immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *dhāraṇī* gates.
It further says: "One shall sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and be born into the family of all Buddhas."
Examine these two conditions closely; do not trouble yourself with further hesitation.

Upon hearing this, the Māra-king resolved to abandon his activities and immediately released Ānanda. Mañjuśrī...

Subhūti, Māra will manifest in the form of a bodhisattva and speak various matters concerning the prediction of a bodhisattva.
Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva conceived a sense of arrogance, thinking, "I have already attained it," and thus disparaged others.
The second fascicle of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-śāstra* (Fu fa zang zhuan) provides a detailed account of the traces of Kūṭadanta; it is now referred to as the *Kūṭadanta Sūtra*.
Upagupta—translated into Chinese as Jìn-hù (Near-Protector)—was a great arhat who attained the six supernormal powers one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

At that time, he served as the great guide for Jambudvīpa. This is seen extensively in that sūtra, as well as in the tenth fascicle of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the one hundred thirty-fifth fascicle of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.

A doubt is raised: If even Ānanda, who had attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), was still disturbed by Māra and required Mañjuśrī to go and rescue him so that he could regain his original mind;
and if Māra can even manifest the body of a Buddha to preach the Dharma to people such that bodhisattvas of shallow practice fail to perceive it—[how much more so for others]?
Venerable Quṭa, you have reached the ultimate path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). Yet when you saw Māra transform himself into a Buddha, you could not avoid taking refuge in him.

Now, you wish to visualize Amitābha so as to see the Buddha at the moment of death; these are all realms of Māra—how can they be relied upon? If what is seen were truly real, it would indeed be a vital medicine.
But if you encounter a demonic image and falsely enter into a heterodox resolution, you will only fall into error.
The true form of the Buddha is a supreme condition for removing illness; the method for causing one to behold it is truly an essential medicine.
The delusive images of heavenly Māras are long-term causes of suffering and evil; teachings that encourage one to encounter them should be considered heterodox doctrines.
His doubts remained unresolved, and he earnestly hoped for an explanation.
Tong said: "The Great Awakened One manifested a provisional form; his divine image is upright and majestic. Although the demon may feign disorder, his likeness is vastly different.

Having practiced diligently through successive kalpas, his supreme causes were fully realized. The fruit of his attainment is the myriad virtues, and his marks and signs are transcendent and extraordinary. How could a wretched demon ever be able to [assume such a form]?"

Regarding "likeness" (*lunni*): its manifestations are not the ultimate reality; therefore, they are called "provisional forms. Because it transcends the realm of thought and deliberation, it is called a "divine image" (*shenxiang*). "Ting" means to transcend; "ba" means to draw forth.
Because it rises loftily above the multitude, it is said to be "towering and eminent" (*tingba*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Buddha [arises] from the immeasurable..."
For incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), he has accumulated great merit until all things are fully perfected. Because the causes and conditions are great, the retribution is likewise great;
other people do not possess this.
Why is this? The Tathāgata’s body is adorned with the purple-gold hue; his marks are fully manifest and brilliant, as clear as bright pearls, and his radiance surpasses ten thousand suns.
Even if the Demon King were to employ transformations, none could alter these marks. This is like the difference between an inferior man and a noble lord.
"Bingran" (Briant) means a radiant appearance. "Fang" (Fang) means comparison.

Ānanda temporarily dwells among the lesser sages; his traces manifest as one who has attained the stage of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*). Yet, according to his actual practice, he has long since ascended to the First Bhūmi.

Anticipating that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, practitioners might have their pure minds corrupted by Māra and find no means to subdue it, [the Buddha] therefore manifested the binding of Māra’s net.

I entreat the Buddha to bestow his majestic power. Once these divine mantras have been proclaimed, they shall serve as the foundation for the teaching, flowing widely through distant ages. Those who study them will subdue Māra;
this does not refer to sages, but rather to ordinary people caught in the net of demonic afflictions.
Ānanda first resolved his mind for enlightenment in the presence of the Buddha Śūnyarāja. Since his practice has long been established, it can be known that he has ascended the stages (bhūmi).

Although there is no textual evidence yet that he has realized the first stage, this clearly indicates that he is indeed on the stages. In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the words of Ānanda’s request are not cited;
the present text refers to him based on such hidden and implicit meanings.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that Māra transforms himself into a Buddha to delude inferior ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

The sūtra further explains that this refers to those who have long failed to practice the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and those who have not yet entered the [bodhisattva] stages (*bhūmi*), thereby indicating that it concerns inferior ordinary beings.

For those bodhisattvas of shallow practice who are unable to fully comprehend this, one should explain the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*. To clarify the provisional manifestation [of the Buddha], the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"Regarding this *Prajñāpāramitā*, if one listens to it, receives and upholds it, draws near to it, reads it, and recites it..."
Even such a person cannot be taken advantage of by Māra or the gods of Māra; therefore, it should be said that this serves to crush Māra.
Ānanda’s demonstration of the disturbances caused by Māra is called "expedient means" (*upāya*). His acting as the catalyst for the arising of the teaching is called "arising."
In the midst of the assembly at the Nirvāṇa, [the Buddha] was requested to explain this. Kāśyapa made this request, saying:
"How can one distinguish between what the Buddha has spoken and what Māra has spoken? The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "It is like a thieving dog that enters a person's house at night;
if the household servants perceive it, they immediately drive it away. The practitioner is also like this: having entered the family of the Buddha, he guards the sweet food and does not allow..."

The demonic is intermingled with the spiritual manifestations of the Buddha, which are exceptionally marvelous and majestic. When Māra comes to confound what is correct, one must skillfully distinguish between them.

The tuft of hair between the eyebrows curls and spirals to the right; it is solid on the outside and hollow within, with white light streaming forth. This light is brilliant and pure, like lapis lazuli. His countenance is perfectly round and luminous, like the gathered sun.
The uṣṇīṣa on his crown is high and prominent, and his hair is a deep azure-blue; each strand of hair is distinct.

A single conch shell, spiraling to the right and winding gracefully—beholding such an auspicious sign, one knows it to be the true form of the Buddha. If it differs from this description, it is a demonic manifestation.
This section summarizes the intent of that scripture; examining the words of Kāśyapa’s inquiry, they originate from the *Dīrghāyuṣ-praśna-sūtra*.
At the beginning of this chapter, the Buddha expounds parables; these appear at the start of the "Four Reliances" (Catuḥpratisaraṇa) chapter.
The practitioner should collect such passages from throughout the sutra, citing them wherever they occur, so that they may be understood upon investigation.
Regarding the statement that Upagupta did not recognize Māra:
the Venerable Upagupta was born after the Buddha; he transmitted the Dharma in succession as the fifth patriarch. He preached the Dharma and delivered sentient beings in great numbers.

The *Dharmaguptaka-dharmakośa-āgama* (Fu fazang zhuan) states: Whenever Upagupta taught the Dharma and brought benefit, if a husband and wife both attained the fruit of Arhatship, he would place down a tally stick (*śalākā*) four inches long.
These were accumulated in a stone chamber measuring over twenty feet in height and over thirty feet in width.
Those who had attained realization individually or as members of other clans were not recorded, even if they were Arhats.
The Māra-king was defiled and debased; though flowers rained down during the Dharma assembly, they disturbed the minds of the multitude, and he was unable to attain realization.

Furthermore, he was to be further deluded; [the Buddha] bestowed upon him a jeweled crown. The Holy One showed compassion and accepted it out of pity. Thereupon, he spoke to the Māra, saying: "I receive this in accordance with the Buddha's teaching."
Understanding the meaning of consciousness and knowing how to repay kindness, the Noble One said, "Since you have bestowed upon me a precious crown, I shall offer you a precious necklace in return.

He then took the corpses of a human, a snake, and a dog, transformed them into a precious necklace, and fastened it around his neck. Pāpīyān rejoiced, saying, "The power of the noble Maudgalyāyana is beyond description;
he transforms and guides all sentient beings, and as a result, such holy companions gather. As for my demonic hosts, they will [be diminished] in turn..."

"Xījiàn, since you have now accepted my precious crown and in turn offered me this precious necklace, Māndhātṛ has fallen into the net of Māra and his descent into evil realms will only increase further.
My own army shall no longer suffer diminution; with my body and mind leaping with joy, I shall immediately return to my palace."

Upon reaching the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, Kūṭadanta withdrew his supernormal powers, and the precious necklaces and jewels were restored to their original state as a corpse—putrid, festering, and bloated with a greenish hue, with pus and blood dripping from it.
Pāpīyas was filled with grief and distress; though he sought to cast it away, there was nowhere to go.
He went throughout the various heavens, wishing to request its removal, but the devas each replied, "This is beyond our power; this is a disciple of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni."
"Upacūḍa, it is because of your ignorance that you have needlessly caused such turmoil. For a moment, I shall subdue your body and mind with this matter;
you must quickly take refuge so that you may escape this calamity. As Pāpīyas descended and approached the Noble One, he prostrated himself with all five limbs in devout sincerity.

In deep sorrow, he offered a repentant apology. The Venerable Kukkuta took pity on him and removed his distress. Addressing the Māra, he said, "I was born after the Buddha’s passing and did not see the Tathāgata.
You should manifest for me the form and marks of the Buddha. The Māra entered a village grove and transformed his body to resemble the Buddha.
Upon seeing this, Kukkuta prepared a seat and prostrated himself in worship. Thereupon, the Māra was struck with alarm and fear, and said to Kukkuta, "Brother..."
"You are but a foolish child. You do not violate my noble teaching; even if you were to transform into a Buddha, you would still remain among the ranks of the common.

The Holy One bowed, saying, "This act of prostration destroys immeasurable merit. The Venerable One replied, "I have recently paid homage to the image of the Buddha, and from afar I revere the Great Master.
You, evil Māra, are not one whom I respect. Do not fear now; do not falsely dread the loss of your merit. Thereupon, King Māra felt deep joy and abandoned all [his concerns].
Engaging in various practices, she took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. She prostrated at the feet of Upagupta and returned to her palace, no longer appearing in person.

Tradition says that she sometimes rained down pure gold, or manifested as a white elephant, or appeared in the form of a woman, so exceptionally beautiful and extraordinary that the entire assembly desired to gaze upon her, yet lacked the intention to listen to the Dharma.
Over the course of twenty-one days, she expounded the flavor of the profound Dharma, even unto [the state of] non-arising.
There was one person who had attained the Way; as the Venerable One entered meditative absorption, he immediately became aware of him.
The *Dacheng yilin zhang* states: "Pāpīyān" means "the Evil One. Regarding the specific name for the celestial Māra, "Pāpīyan" is a corruption. He leads an army of twelve thousand five hundred men;
this refers to leading his hosts to wage war against Heaven and Earth, which is why they are called an "army host. To "control" (kòng) means to lead.
Furthermore, during the twenty-one days [of the funeral rites], he was not aware of being disturbed by Māra; therefore, it is said that he was "without knowledge.

Alternatively, it may be that Pāpīyān did not yet know of the Venerable One’s supernatural power, and thus it was called "without knowledge" in this sense. *Cuo* (挫) means to crush or defeat. *Yōng* (庸) means ordinary or constant.
When a person of humble status offers greetings, they say "I pay homage" (*wénán*); this is here termed "reverence" (*gōngjìng*).
How could one doubt that such words do not recognize the existence of Māra?

Furthermore, it is like when a multitude of high-ranking officials lend their strength to a single man; no wicked person can then invade or disturb him. It is the same for those who practice cultivation:
if they cultivate mindfulness with utmost sincerity, they will certainly be reborn there, and all the Buddhas of the ten directions will collectively bestow their supportive power.

Spirit! At the time when your retribution is exhausted, no demon shall be able to disturb you. Amitābha transforms the multitudes, universally radiating his compassionate light to receive and guide your soul and emotions, causing them to ascend to the Land of Wondrous Bliss.
Do not fear demonic interference; do not fail to cultivate wholesome causes.
The *Sūtra of the Small Perfection of Wisdom* states: "One is protected and mindful of by all Buddhas. The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states:

"By reciting the Buddha’s name with a loud voice, the demonic armies will retreat and scatter. The *Sūtra of Praise* states: "Through the empowerment of compassion, one's mind shall not be disturbed."
The seventh [comparison] contrasts the Pure Land of the West with Maitreya’s heavenly palace to reveal their relative merits.
Tiantai, Jiacai, and Daochuo each analyzed them according to the principles of two, three, and four [aspects], respectively.
Master Gan also explained this using twelve [points]. Ancient masters of former generations have extensively debated this matter, likely because many people were concerned about it.

This gives rise to delusion. The Vinaya Master raises a doubt, saying: "The *Commentary on the Sūtra of Rebirth Above* states that there are ten easy births in the celestial palaces, whereas there are seven difficult births in the Pure Land.
Furthermore, it encourages [rebirth in] the Inner Court, saying: 'Even if one's karmic practice is shallow, one should aspire to be born in the Western Paradise.'"

If one does not practice, there is the fear of bringing about one's own ruin; therefore, one must act now and should cultivate this karma. How is it that the interpretation of a single master is so [different]?
Thus we know that this book was not composed by Master Jizang. Now, Huìyuǎn says:

"The teachings spoken by the Tathāgata differ in ten thousand ways according to the capacities of sentient beings; the masters who expound the teachings likewise manifest them according to emptiness. Entering through any single gate," and so forth.

They all return to a single principle. This is the intent of what is described in this text. Therefore, even within the *Tongzan* (General Praise), ten superior practices are cited specifically to encourage the Pure Land;
each follows its own path, and none are mutually contradictory.
An objection states: "The Pure Land of Amitābha is distant from here, whereas Maitreya’s heavenly palace currently resides within the desire realm.
Why not aspire to be born in Tuṣita instead of heading toward the West? To abandon what is easy and seek what is difficult—is this not circuitous and obstructive?"
"Yū" (迂) means winding and crooked; it signifies stagnation and delay.
[The Master] said: "In comparing the two conditions, there are many varieties. I shall briefly set forth ten differences to collectively resolve the doubts of the assembly."
1. Life spans differ in length; 2. Abodes differ in being internal or external; 3. Objects differ in being defiled or pure; 4. Physical retributions differ in two ways;
5. The manifestations of the seeds differ; 6. Advancement and retreat differ in cultivation; 7. Realms differ from non-realms; 8. Beautiful and ugly forms differ in appearance.
Ninth, the relinquishing of life differs; tenth, the exhortations in the sutras vary in length.

First, regarding the longevity of their lives: the lifespan in Tuṣita is only four thousand years, whereas the lifespan in the Western [Pure Land] is one hundred ten-million-billion nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Four hundred years among humans constitute one day and night for that heaven.
By human reckoning, this amounts to fifty billion, sixty thousand, nayuta—here translated as "ten billion"—and asaṃkhyeya—here translated as "incalculable.
As stated in the Great Fundamental Vow regarding lifespan: "Should there be anyone capable of measuring it, down to even hundreds of thousands of billions of nayuta kalpas."
"I shall not attain perfect enlightenment. The *Sūtra of the Smaller Version* states: "For immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) kalpas.
Although the present [text] regarding Śākyamuni speaks of "incalculable" (*asaṃkhyeya*), it does not say "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*). How could this contradict the sūtras?

For the *Mahā-amitābha-sūtra*, the *Sūtra of Equal Enlightenment*, the *Sūtra of Compassionate Flowers*, the *Puṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and others all state that there is a definite measure. Therefore, for the time being, we rely on one such account to harmonize it with the [celestial]...
In the *Shoudui lun* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts), the master is even judged to be a *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body); how could he then be immeasurable?
If one follows the *Tongzan* (General Praise), it likewise judges him to be immeasurable, as this preserves the sense of the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body).
Regarding the two locations, inner and outer: if one’s wisdom-karma (*prajñā-karman*) is predominant, one is born in the inner location, personally attending Maitreya;

if wisdom is slight and merit (*puṇya*) is predominant, one is born in the outer location and does not see the Compassionate Honored One. Within the Pure Land, there is no distinction between inner and outer;

The period following the first five hundred years constitutes the third stage; this refers to the teaching of the True Dharma (*saddharma*) during the subsequent five hundred years.

The period after the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*) is the third stage. In terms of location, the Pure Land is the first stage, for in that world of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), there is no turbidity and only the One Vehicle is taught. Since the One Vehicle is the dharma of the first stage, it is therefore designated as such.
The first level is the Sahā world of defilement; this is the second level, the world of the Three Vehicles, which possesses these five turbidities.
By dividing the One Vehicle into three, the Three Vehicles constitute the Dharma of the second level; therefore, it is designated as the second level.

It is also a place where precepts are violated and views are corrupted; as it is the characteristic of the third stage where both precepts and views are destroyed, it is likewise designated as the third stage.
Regarding the individuals [who belong there], those of the first stage are of two kinds:

first, those who—regardless of whether they are ordinary persons or sages—possess both precepts and views, have achieved right view, and are of all sharp faculties, possessing the capacity for the One Vehicle.

Regarding the faculties: there are two types of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Second, do not inquire into all instances of broken precepts; rather, [note that] there is one kind who has never corrupted right view.

There are two kinds of ordinary beings with sharp faculties and Bodhisattvas with the capacity for the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), yet these are exclusively those of the most superior, sharp faculties who possess the capacity for the One Vehicle. Within the second stage, although they also bear the name [of Bodhisattva],...
As for the "One Vehicle" (Ekayāna), it still does not transcend the Three Vehicles. Regarding the second grade of capacity, there are also two types:

These are ordinary persons who have entirely broken their precepts but not their views.

Although sentient beings comprise these two categories, they are both of sharp faculties and right view, constituting the potential for the three vehicles. Regarding the third stage, the citations in the collected records are extremely extensive;
upon careful examination, it is clear that this category consists solely of those who have broken both precepts and views and are entirely inverted.

Sentient beings belong to the third stage of capacity. If discussed in terms of time, although this is so, when discussing individuals, it is possible for those of the third stage of capacity to exist throughout the present age and even prior to five hundred years [after the Buddha’s passing].

Furthermore, it is also possible for those of the first and second stages of capacity to exist after one thousand years have passed. Moreover, although the capacity of those in the Sahā world is indeed of the third stage, [it is not fixed].

Regarding the discussion of persons, there are likewise two [categories]. Other matters concerning their general or specific application should be understood by analogy. This is explained in detail in the *Jilu* (Collection of Records).

Regarding the three poisons: now that you have focused your mind on the Buddha with the vow to go to the Western Land, your perverse poisons have instead increased; is this not a perverted view?

Or they are born among humans and devas; thus they revolve through the six realms of existence, suffering endlessly. Because they grasp at objects in a distorted manner, they are called "perverse" (*mithyā*).

These three poisons are accumulated within the field of the mind. Even if one practices mindfulness of the Buddha, if spirits, ghosts, and demons are provoked, how can one attain rebirth in the Pure Land?

This is indeed a matter of doubt; there is truly a reason for it. Tong said:

"The purport of the teachings is of a transcendent order. All desire to benefit sentient beings; knowing well what to adopt and what to reject, each acts according to the specific conditions and capacities of others."

Why is this? If one has realized the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpāda*), it is possible to dwell long in the Sahā world; however, until one has attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), it is difficult to remain in a defiled land.
If one accords with non-arising, then Sukhāvatī and the Sahā world are non-dual; thus, there is no need to loathe this impure realm and separately yearn for the Pure Land.

As for the location, it is situated within saṃsāra; one must necessarily be born there. It is the impure land where Great Beings (mahāsattvas) dwell; those with understanding should constantly frequent it without interruption.
Those of inferior capacity who have not yet perfected the sublime contemplation (vipaśyanā) will, upon briefly resting there, return once more to the long-flowing stream of suffering.

Internally, one accumulates the three roots of goodness; externally, one summons the assistance of the multitude of sages. When the retribution of this world finally ends, the pure lotuses of the wondrous land will come to welcome one.

The three impurities (*mala*) are extinguished, the mind becomes supple, and wholesome thoughts emerge. How could such radiant benefit possibly be in vain?

The noble assembly of the Three Vehicles, out of compassion for sentient beings, should realize that they are identical in essence to ordinary people; yet, failing to recognize this—like those born blind—they instead harbor contempt and suppression, thereby increasing the conditions for evil.

or, according to what is attained in dhyāna, the samādhis practiced by ordinary persons that are not the sixfold meditative absorptions (*ṣaḍ-ākāra-dhyāna*). These are the six types of meditative absorption.
Because those who are concentrated will necessarily be reborn in the higher realms, dwelling deeply in hearing and reflection is also called *samādhi*.

Furthermore, reciting and chanting the scriptures, expounding them, and practicing the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*)—these six matters represent the most prominent and easily practiced primary factors.
Each one of these six fully encompasses all other activities; if one practices all six, or even five of them, one will be reborn in the highest of the high grades.
If one cultivates three or four [levels] of superior or middle-grade rebirth, or if one cultivates one or two [levels] of superior, middle, or lower-grade rebirth;
and if those born through the next three grades of conduct— namely, the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings who have not previously violated the precepts,

nor committed evil, and whose offenses are minor— hear the name and their minds rejoice, their speech expresses reverence, and their bodies perform prostrations, then among these, one who possesses all three types of action is of middle-superior grade.
Birth occurs solely through two types of karma: middling-middling birth, or if there is only one type of karma, it is middling-low birth.

Furthermore, regarding birth through the three lower grades of practice, although there are ten practices, they are subsumed into six: first, repentance; second, making images; third, making offerings; fourth, prostration;
