Although the various teachings on the Path differ according to the capacities of those to be guided, they cause one to awaken to and enter the ineffable nature of reality (dharmatā), which is of a single uniform flavor like salt and entirely without distinction.
Next, regarding the phrase "the perfect luminosity of original enlightenment" (*mūla-bodhi*), there are two interpretations in recent general commentaries; first, by means of clarity...

It is unreasonable to claim that what is called the "Assembly of the Pure Dharma-realm" refers to *mūla-bodhi* (original enlightenment). The preceding sentence states that the essence of *tathatā* (suchness) is pure, which is the pure *dharmadhātu*.
To say this again—that *mūla-bodhi* is the perfectly luminous *dharmadhātu* realized by the Buddha as true purity—is redundant.

If one were to offer a defense, saying that the purity of the essence of *tathatā* constitutes *prakṛti-viśuddha-nirvāṇa* (naturally pure nirvana), while *mūla-bodhi* as perfect luminosity is the *dharmadhātu* of true purity realized by the Buddha, [the fault remains].

It is unreasonable to claim that the basis for transformation is equal [to the dharmadhātu]. The statement "perfectly luminous" (pariśuddha) explains this principle by way of being free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), yet it does not clarify that primordial purity (*ādi-viśuddhi*) and *nirvāṇa* are likewise free from conceptual proliferation; thus, this explanation is redundant. Therefore, the first interpretation is unsuitable for resolving the difficulty.
Next, explaining it as the existence of innate, untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) is more appropriate. Nevertheless, even this explanation does not clarify the meaning. Now...

The commentary explains that "original" refers to original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), which is right gnosis (*samyag-jñāna*). Its essence consists of the mental states of the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna-citta-varga*).

As stated in the tenth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, these mental states of the four wisdoms possess the seeds capable of producing them as their "original" [cause], and they are attained through what is produced.

Thus, the four wisdoms are here termed "original enlightenment. When the four wisdoms are perfectly luminous, the fruit of Buddhahood is manifested. The preceding phrase [refers] to pure phenomena (*viśuddha-dharma*).

The first phrase, "the realm is the essence of true suchness," indicates that it is pure by nature. The subsequent phrase, "the four wisdoms are manifest as the perfect clarity of original enlightenment," is as stated in the *Dharmaparyāya-ṭīkā* (Commentary on the Abhidharma) in its verse of homage:

"I bow my head to the perfectly clear and tranquil original nature. The term "perfectly clear" (*yuanming*) reveals the four wisdoms, while the term "tranquil original nature" (*xingben ji*) manifests the pure dharma-realm (*viśuddha-dharmadhātu*).
Apart from the pure dharma-realm, there is no manifestation of the fruit of Buddhahood within the categories of the four wisdoms.
Therefore, this is fully as explained in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*.

Furthermore, regarding the recent common interpretation that resolves the doubt by stating that all things equally return to a single reality (*ekasatya*) by identifying the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) with the single reality, this is not the intent of our school.

Our school’s teaching on the term "single reality" refers to setting aside the provisional expression (*prajñapti*) to discuss the ultimate principle (*artha*); the single reality is suchness (*tathatā*).

The *Treatise on the Definitive Meaning of the Name "Pure Dharma-realm"* (*Qingjing fajie ming liaoyi deng*) and other texts state that the essence of the Tathāgata’s established teachings is the single true thusness (*tathatā*);
this accords with the intent of the present [work].

Furthermore, regarding the doubt as to whether [the Bodhisattva] has regressed from Tuṣita or not, recent general explanations maintain that although there is generally regression for the majority, [in this case...]
There is a point that has not yet been clearly understood; now I shall explain it in detail. The *Shangsheng shu* (Commentary on the Higher Birth) states:

"If one is born among the external assemblies, although [the stage] may be the lowest of the low, at a later time one will spontaneously become a non-retrogressive Buddha, named Maitreya, because one’s own cultivation has flourished" (and so forth).

Since this passage says "at a later time one will again become [a Buddha]," it serves as proof that there is retrogression at that stage. If there was no retrogression previously, on what basis can you say [there is none]?
At a later time, they may again attain it; the word "again" (huan) indicates that although there is regression, through the power of Maitreya’s empowerment, one regains non-regression.
"Attainment" (cheng) means to acquire. Furthermore, once one has been reborn in the Pure Land of the West, there is never any regression thereafter.

Comparing this with the present *Yaojue* (Essential Decision), it says: "There is regression in the heavens above, but none in the West; how much more so when it is said that [regression] is frequent [in the heavens]."

Since it is unavoidable that there are those who regress, and because the statement "for the most part" indicates that there are also some who do not regress, there is no contradiction whatsoever between these two passages.
Furthermore, regarding the presence or absence of the welcoming [deities], the recent general interpretation—which attempts to distinguish them based on superiority or inferiority—is inappropriate.

Now, examining the *Sūtra on Rebirth Above* (*Ūrdhvasrotas-sūtra*), it states that there are three types of conduct for rebirth; these modes of rebirth consist of both general and specific characteristics.
Because it is difficult to distinguish [the specific details], the Master of the Commentary (*Śāstrin*) divides them into nine grades to clarify the distinctions between birth through practice.

Among these, regarding the lower grade of the upper birth, he speaks only of the signs of Maitreya’s coming to welcome one; for the other eight grades of birth through practice, he does not mention this.

In the Pure Land of the West, although the welcoming of those born in the lower grade of the middle birth is not mentioned as being personally led by [Amitābha], it is stated for all the other eight grades.
Regarding the description of seeing golden lotuses in the case of the lowest grade of the lowest birth (*adhamādhamā-upapatti*), this is also a sign of being welcomed [by the Buddhas].
Now, in this *Yōketsu*, the welcoming is explained primarily in relation to the nine grades of rebirth; it states that if one is born in the Pure Land, the holy assembly will come to welcome them.

Furthermore, regarding those born in the upper-middle six grades or the outer precincts of the lowest-lowest grade, there is no sign of being welcomed at the moment of casting off life. It says: "At the time of death..."

Regarding those born in the heavens, there is no one to guide them, and few belong [to the path] because they lack [the necessary conditions]. (The above concludes the resolution of the five doubts concerning the chamber of Nanyue).
Next, regarding the judgment of the second school’s doubts: within this text, it is permitted that ordinary beings attain rebirth;
furthermore, citing old translations while not citing new ones serves as a point of doubt and difficulty. Recent exegeses clarify that by the power of the Original Vow, the five vehicles are unified.

Regarding the meaning of ordinary beings being born in the Reward Land (*vipākakṣetra*), it is said that they are encompassed by the Original Vow (*pūrvapraṇidhāna*) but are not determined by *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) and are not subsumed under the categories of nature (*svabhāva*) or characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, since this treatise speaks of being born in the Transformation Land (*nirmāṇakṣetra*) and seeing transformation Buddhas (*nirmāṇabuddha*), it cites the three principles of our own school to harmonize them with the meanings of the Reward and Transformation lands.
As for those who harbor doubts, what is their ignorance? Now, to examine this in detail: [The text continues with the detailed analysis.]

This commentary does not clarify my school’s judgment that the Reward and Transformation bodies of An-yang (Sukhāvatī) have three meanings: first, exclusively reward; second, exclusively transformation;

and third, encompassing both reward and transformation. The Master Hai-zhu of Mount Shang determined the third meaning to be correct, and to this day, the students of the Abhidharma school in Nanjing rely upon this interpretation.
Now, I shall extract its essentials and examine them: if it were [exclusively]...
The teaching of the Noble Ones states that the land of retribution—which is not a land of transformation—is what is seen by *sattvas* on the ground; it is not within the reach of ordinary beings.

If an ordinary person, through the power of their vows, were to say they are born spontaneously in a land of retribution and see a Buddha of retribution there—such as Amitābha Buddha manifesting a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) in a land of transformation—then a land of transformation would be entirely useless. If a land of transformation were useless, then the Buddha’s original vow would likewise be so.
It would follow that he is not a Buddha perfected in the three bodies (*trikāya*), and thus the sense of being solely a *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) is untenable.

Furthermore, if he were merely a *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) and not a *saṃbhogakāya*, there would be no distinction between him and other Buddhas who likewise cause ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) to be born in a land of emanation;

how then could he be called Amitābha, whose special vows transcend the world? Therefore, the position that he is merely an emanation is untenable. Consequently, it is correct to say that he is both a *saṃbhogakāya* and a *nirmāṇakāya*. Why is this so?

Regarding the attainment of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), it is explained in general that there are two types of transformation lands (*nirmāṇa-kṣetra*): first, long-term transformations; second, temporary transformations. The pure land of the West is a land of universal transformation;

it is a long-term transformation because it manifests as the Land of Reward (*vipāka-bhūmi*). Since there is no manifestation apart from the reward, this is also because it is a long-term transformation in fulfillment of the power of the original vow.
If one speaks of transformation in terms of returning to the fundamental nature (*dharmatā*), then the land of reward is that which transcends other Buddhas.

Therefore, it is said that these are the extraordinary vows that transcend the world. However, this *Yaojue* (Essential Decision) states that one is born in the Land of Transformation and sees the Buddha of Transformation;

it further says that by seeking to see the Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya), one consequently moves Maitreya—the Lord of Transformation—to descend and extend his thought to welcome [the practitioner].

These statements are made with reference to the three lower grades [of rebirth], wherein the Buddha of Transformation, the Transformation Avalokiteśvara, and the Transformation Mahāsthāmaprāpta arrive at the practitioner.

For this reason, treatises such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra* state that the nirmāṇakāya (emanation body) still relies upon a nirmāṇabhūmi (emanation land), because there is no possibility for a body to exist apart from its land.
For now, we shall consider the attainment of benefit according to the three lower grades, which involves being born in an emanation land and seeing an emanation Buddha;
this is not contradictory in principle, even though it is a fulfillment of the vows of an emanation Buddha that is unique compared to other Buddhas.

Question: If that is so, why does this definitive text state that the emanator (nirmāṇa-prabhu) attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) by taking [the emanated being] by the hand?
Answer: The patience of non-arising refers to the benefit of the three superior grades; how could this contradict [that]? Answer:

There are two aspects to the term "patience of non-arising" as commonly discussed in the established doctrines: first, it refers to [the attainment] from the eighth bhūmi upward; second, it refers to [the attainment] from the first bhūmi upward. The former...
Regarding what is taught in the three grades— that the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is spoken of in the three grades above and below the eighth stage—
since it is stated that one has already entered the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*) in the middle grade of the superior birth,

this definitive conclusion that one enters the first stage is entirely consistent with the principle of attaining the patience of non-arising. Furthermore, regarding the failure to cite the new translations concerning rebirth in the Western [Pure Land]:
Since this work is dedicated exclusively to the old translations, I have cited only the old translations to provide the explanations and establish the proofs.
Question: If that is so, the *Sūtra on Rebirth in the Upper Realm* (*Śūramgama-samādhi-sūtra*) is also an old translation; why then do you cite both new and old versions in your commentary? Answer:

The commentary on the *Sūtra on Rebirth in the Upper Realm* is intended to explain and establish the meaning of the sūtra itself; therefore, it cites both new and old versions. However, this present work, the *Essential Determination*, establishes its arguments solely through reasoning rather than providing an explanatory commentary.
Because this is based on the sūtras, it cites only the principles of the ancient sūtras; thus, there is no contradiction with the sūtras.

Question: Is the principle established by recent general exegesis—that what is subsumed under the original vows is not determined by the *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) doctrine and is not subsumed within either the nature (*svabhāva*) or the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*)—correct? Answer: The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu established that all phenomena are *vijñaptimātra*.

The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and other scriptures teach that all phenomena are consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). Therefore, this [system] encompasses all phenomena, both contaminated and uncontaminated, as is clearly explained in the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-ṭīkā* and other works.
That is to say, the Buddha’s original vows are transformations upon the Buddha’s own consciousness and thus serve as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*);
consequently, for a practitioner of Buddha-recollection, the mental image of rebirth manifests upon their own mental consciousness.

How can it be said that this is not determined by the doctrine of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only)? If one were to insist that the Buddha’s vows are not transformations of consciousness-only, then one would necessarily hold fast to the existence of a real Buddha-mind.
But how could there be such an insistence? Furthermore, the Buddha’s original vow states: "That which is not subsumed within nature (*svabhāva*) or characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*)...

If it is beyond nature and characteristics, what further discussion can there be? If there is nothing to discuss, then let it be; yet, for the sake of expediency, one might provisionally give rise to words concerning nature and characteristics.

Furthermore, since the inconceivable and extraordinary vows of Amida that transcend the world are beyond the reach of verbal discourse, it is said that "nature and characteristics have not yet been distinguished.
This refers to the single Dharma-realm, which is the "True Suchness" (tathatā) of our own school where the provisional means are discarded to discuss the ultimate intent.
If one relies on the gate of the provisional means, then nature and characteristics remain distinct; however, once the gate of the provisional means is discarded...

It is said that when one abandons verbal expression to manifest the underlying principle, what basis can there be for it? What aspiration can there be? To forcefully apply the designation "original vow" (hon-gwan) is merely a name.

If there were a separate, fixed original vow that manifested before one and established some slight entity, claiming this to be the power of the original vow, then because it involves something attained, it would not be the true original vow of the Buddha; it could only be called the view established by the Hīnayāna, not the Mahāyāna.
To claim that because they are viewed from the perspective of the vehicle (yāna), the nature and characteristics (lakṣaṇa) are not subsumed, is a false judgment.

Furthermore, the third school raises a doubt based on the statement that the three bodies (trikāya) are non-different; recent scholars have attempted to reconcile this by subsuming characteristics into nature.

I maintain, however, that this does not fully resolve the matter. As stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Cheng weishi lun), Chapter 10, there are three distinct types of dharma-body (dharmakāya): first, the self-...
The nature body (*svābhāvika-kāya*), the two enjoyment bodies (*sambhoga-kāya*), and the transformation body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*)—these three bodies together constitute the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Because they are all adorned by the unsurpassed, silent Dharma, they cannot be separated. This is precisely the three bodies established in our own school;
thus, it is entirely without contradiction that the three bodies are not different.

Someone asked: "Since the calligraphic style (*bi-ge*) of this book does not resemble that of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-ṭīkā* and other works, there remains some doubt; what should be done about it? The answer was:

"The calligraphic styles of the commentaries (*zhang-sū*) by Ci'en are not uniform. Once the Master himself had proofread and corrected them, the calligraphic styles became consistent, as seen in the thirty-fascicle and twenty-fascicle *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-ṭīkā*, the *Yilin zhang*, and so forth.
However, there may still be passages that have not been proofread, such as those in the *Dafayuan yi chao* (Six)."
From this point downward, there may be passages where only the Master spoke and the disciples recorded it, such as in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra-śāstra* and other works.

It is feared that this book, too, was produced by the hands of the disciples; its literary style is entirely lax and deviates from the main intent. One must certainly verify it against other commentaries and treatises;
it should not be regarded as beyond doubt.
Although there are certainly errors in what has been set forth above, I have recorded these notes at random with my clumsy intellect,
solely for the purpose of causing sentient beings to give rise to a resolute conviction that loathes this defiled land and desires the Pure Land.
May this slight merit be universally bestowed upon all living beings, increasing their resolve for world-weariness and enabling them to be born in that [Pure Land] by virtue of the Buddha’s vow.
*Discerning the Authenticity of the Essentials for Rebirth in the Western Paradise: Resolving Doubts* (End).
